title: CFA Alternatives 2: Why ordinary performance measures give the wrong answer for this group
subtitle: Return smoothing, stale prices, and three biases that make hedge fund indices look better than reality
openingQuestion: A property fund reports a standard deviation of returns far below listed equities. Which conclusion is correct?
openingOptions: Property really is less risky than listed equities
The figure is smoothed because valuation is by periodic appraisal
That fund manages risk better than a conventional equity fund does
Standard deviation cannot be applied to property
explanation: The asset is appraised each quarter, and the appraiser takes their reference from the previous valuation plus a few recent comparable transactions. The result is that the reported series of values moves slowly even when the real market has swung hard - the phenomenon called return smoothing. The measurement consequences are very specific: standard deviation is understated, correlation with other asset groups is understated, so the Sharpe ratio and the apparent diversification benefit both look better than reality. This is not fraud - it is a structural consequence of there being no continuous market price.

diagram.label: Sharpe and the diversification benefit look better than reality

realWorldExample.company: The three biases of a hedge fund index
realWorldExample.description: A hedge fund index is built from data funds volunteer, and that creates three biases all pointing the same way. Survivorship bias: funds that close because of poor results stop reporting and drop out of the index. Self-selection bias: a fund doing well wants to be known, a fund doing badly does not. And instant history bias: a fund newly joining is allowed to load its whole past return series, and a fund only does that when the series looks good. All three push the index up, so it is not something a real investor could have achieved.

quiz.question: Where does return smoothing come from?
options: From valuing by periodic appraisal instead of at market price
From the fund deliberately adjusting reported figures to look better
From returns being computed annually rather than monthly
From the management fee being spread evenly across reporting periods
quiz.explanation: This is a structural consequence, not a behaviour. The appraiser anchors on the previous valuation, so the series of values is always smoother than reality. No deliberate adjustment is needed for the effect to appear, and it shows up just as clearly in monthly data as in annual.

quiz.question: How does return smoothing affect the risk measures?
options: Standard deviation is overstated while correlation is understated
Both standard deviation and correlation are understated
It only affects the average return, not the risk
No effect at all if the data series is long enough
quiz.explanation: Both measures are pulled down, so the Sharpe ratio and the diversification benefit are exaggerated at the same time. Length of series does not cure it: smoothing is a bias, not noise, so more observations make the wrong number more precise rather than more correct.

quiz.question: What is instant history bias in a hedge fund index?
options: Historical data is deleted after a number of years under retention rules
The index is fully recomputed whenever a new fund joins it
A new fund loads its whole past series, and only when it looks good
Funds must report their return on the day the period ends
quiz.explanation: This is a bias specific to the voluntary reporting mechanism, and it compounds with survivorship bias and self-selection bias. The problem is not the recomputation itself but the selection: a fund with a poor past record simply never joins, so the history that gets added is never a random sample.

quiz.question: Why is IRR hard to compare between a private equity fund and a listed equity fund?
options: Because IRR can only be computed once the fund has fully exited
Because IRR does not account for the management fee the fund charges annually
Because listed funds are not permitted to publish an IRR figure
Because IRR depends on when capital is called and returned, decided by the GP
quiz.explanation: The GP controls the flows in and out, so IRR measures timing skill as well as investment skill - while a listed fund's time-weighted return does not. Interim IRRs are published all the time before exit, and net-of-fee IRRs are standard, so neither of those is the obstacle.

quiz.question: What is the practical consequence of not correcting for these biases?
options: Allocating capital on a risk level lower than the real one
Mis-estimating the management fee payable to the fund each year
Being unable to compare two funds within the same strategy group
Missing newly formed funds that lack enough operating history
quiz.explanation: This is why the lesson matters: the distortion does not sit in one isolated number, it sits in the portfolio allocation decision itself. Fees are disclosed separately and are unaffected by smoothing, and funds within one group are distorted alike, so comparing them to each other is the one thing that still works.

keyTakeaways: Smoothing is a structural consequence of appraisal valuation, not fraud
It pulls down both standard deviation and correlation, so Sharpe is exaggerated
Hedge fund indices have three biases pointing the same way: survivorship, self-selection, instant history
A PE fund's IRR measures timing skill too, because the GP controls the cash flows
Uncorrected, you allocate capital on a level of risk lower than the real one

practicePrompt.question: You are comparing a property fund (reported standard deviation 6%) with an equity fund (18%) to choose portfolio weights. What should you do first?
options: Pick the property fund, its risk is three times lower
Correct for the smoothing before making the comparison
Ignore standard deviation, compare average returns
Ask the fund to republish its figures monthly
practicePrompt.explanation: Comparing the two numbers directly compares valuation frequency rather than risk, and it always tilts towards the illiquid asset. The standard industry treatment is to unsmooth the return series, or to use a listed property index as a reference - both of which push the true standard deviation up to nearly double the reported figure.

summary.keyIdea: A handsome Sharpe in this asset class is usually a consequence of HOW IT IS VALUED rather than of management skill - and that is a reading error, not the fund manager's fault.
summary.commonMistake: Reading an alternative fund's Sharpe the way you read an equity fund's. The denominator has already been compressed before the division happens.

application.title: The cheapest tell
application.message: Unusually positive autocorrelation in the return series. Real market prices have almost no meaningful autocorrelation.

sections.text: The Sharpe ratio, standard deviation and correlation coefficient all assume a trustworthy series of market prices. In the alternative asset group that assumption does not hold - and every measure built on it is skewed in the same direction: flattering.

The asset is appraised each quarter, and the appraiser takes their reference from the previous valuation plus a few recent comparable transactions. The result is that the reported series of values moves slowly even when the real market has swung hard. This is not fraud - it is a structural consequence of there being no continuous price.

sections.label: The measurement consequence
sections.text: Standard deviation is understated and correlation with other groups is understated too. These two errors point the same way, so the Sharpe ratio is exaggerated AND the diversification benefit looks larger than it really is.
The three biases of a hedge fund index

items: Survivorship bias: funds that close stop reporting, so only the winners are left in the index.
Self-selection bias: reporting is voluntary, and a fund doing badly has little reason to report.
Instant history bias: a newly joining fund gets to fill in its whole handsome past record.

sections.text: All three push the index return higher than reality, and they compound rather than cancel out. Private equity funds have a further problem of their own: IRR depends on when capital is called and returned, and those are things the fund manager controls - so IRR measures timing skill and not only investment skill.

lines: Uncorrected, you allocate capital on a level of risk lower than the real one.
And you discover that at exactly the moment you need to get your money out.
